synopsis: Automatic braking introduces hazards of its own: sudden operator jolts, load spill, rollover or articulation instability, sliding, secondary collisions and rollaway; allowable interventions depend on the machine and operating situation [f114, f5941, f7456, f1539]. Moving from warning to intervention turns a false classification into a machine-motion command, while nuisance stops can encourage disabling or bypass and ultimately remove protection when needed [f3024, f11706, f11764]. The booklet recommends separately analyzing missed interventions and unsafe or unnecessary interventions, assigning each its own acceptance thresholds and including both in the simulation matrix [f2642, f8203]. ISO 19014-2:2022 brings brake-command integrity, faults, degraded modes and unintended activation into validation, but no off-road standard prescribing the balance between the two intervention categories was found [f5223, f8204]. On-road evidence identifies unnecessary braking as the dominant documented failure mode and reports a 20% increase in being struck from behind, whereas off-road intervention-created risks remain unmeasured: workers report jolting stops, the regulator knows of no resulting injuries, and evidence of braking-caused load spills, slope instability or rear-end strikes was not found [f115, f11674, f3025, f3026, f3027, f3031]. Important validation gaps remain: no safe maximum automatic deceleration for articulated machines was found, warning-product field evidence does not establish braking consequences, and passive shadow recording cannot prove them [f6555, f7945, f5737].
